title: Representational Similarity and Model Behavior in Multi-Agent Interaction
one_liner: Measure how similar two models are internally and show that higher similarity helps cooperation while reducing originality.
lead: When two language models work together, their success depends not only on raw capability but also on how similarly they organize language and concepts. This paper studies that relation directly across many model pairs and many interaction games. The main result is a tradeoff: pairs with more similar internal representations cooperate better, while pairs with less similar representations produce more original outputs. That tradeoff matters because agent design often assumes that stronger individual models automatically make stronger teams, even though team behavior also depends on how well the members align internally.

problem.h2: Why team behavior cannot be predicted from single-model scores alone
paras: Two models can perform well on their own and still work poorly together. In cooperative tasks, a pair needs compatible ways of parsing words, instructions, and intermediate statements. In creative tasks, some mismatch can help because the pair explores different directions instead of repeating the same one.

That means pair design needs a quantity beyond standalone accuracy. The paper studies representational similarity as that quantity because it may explain why some pairs coordinate smoothly while others produce broader but less aligned outputs.

callout.html: Use internal similarity between two models to predict pair behavior, because shared internal structure can help coordination and reduce diversity at the same time.

steps.text: Pair different language models so the study covers a wide range of capability gaps and internal similarity levels.
Compare representations across early, middle, and later layers because different stages may matter differently for interaction.
Evaluate how well each pair aligns on shared-goal games so the study can measure coordinated success.
Evaluate how varied or creative each pair becomes so the study can measure the cost of too much similarity.
Separate similarity effects from size and capability differences because the claim is about internal alignment, not only raw strength.

paras: The paper changes multi-agent analysis from asking only how strong each model is to asking how similar the pair is internally.
object.object: the predictor used to explain pair behavior

hidden.name: pairwise representational similarity
paras: The hidden quantity is how similarly two models encode the same inputs. This is not visible from the final chat alone because two pairs can produce similar outputs even when one pair reached them through closely aligned internal states and the other through very different ones.

The paper finds that higher similarity, especially in early layers, is associated with better cooperation. That likely happens because early processing shapes shared lexical and semantic grounding, so both models attach similar structure to the same prompts and intermediate messages.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark factors that rise when two models interpret inputs in closely aligned ways.

reads.html: This quantity asks whether the two models see the task in a similar internal way. Higher similarity helps them coordinate because they attach similar meaning to the same messages.
Layer-wise representational similarity predicts interaction outcomes, with early-layer similarity showing the strongest association with cooperation and originality tradeoffs.

mechanism.h2: Why similarity helps coordination and hurts originality
paras: Cooperation improves when two models organize language and task cues similarly because one model's intermediate message is then easier for the other to interpret as intended. Shared grounding reduces coordination errors, so the pair can spend less effort repairing misunderstandings.

Originality can fall for the same reason. If both models map prompts into similar internal structures, they are more likely to propose related continuations and related plans. That reduces the range of explored directions because the pair starts from similar internal assumptions.

Early layers matter most because they shape basic word and concept processing. If those foundations align, later interaction has a stable common base. If they diverge early, later coordination has more opportunities to drift even when the models are individually strong.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Pair A has similarity 8 on a ten-point scale, while Pair B has similarity 3.
In a cooperation task with coop_weight = 4 and originality_weight = 1, Pair A gets more coordination benefit because 4 * 8 is larger than 4 * 3.
In an originality task, the same Pair A loses more diversity because 1 * 8 is larger than 1 * 3.
So Pair A is the stronger choice for strict coordination tasks.
Pair B can be the stronger choice for idea-generation tasks because its lower similarity preserves more varied directions.

math.note: The actual analysis is statistical and layer-wise, but the core tradeoff is simple: similarity helps alignment because shared internal structure reduces misread messages, and it reduces diversity because both models start from more similar assumptions.

items.b: Similarity can be confounded with shared training data.
items.html: If two models are similar because they were built from very similar data and design choices, the measured relation may partly reflect common origin rather than a universal interaction law.

items.b: The task choice may change the tradeoff.
items.html: A task that needs both close coordination and fresh ideas may not fit the simple similarity-versus-originality split because it demands both alignment and variation at different stages.

items.b: Similarity metrics may miss useful differences.
items.html: If the metric compresses internal structure too aggressively, two pairs can look equally similar even when one shares task-relevant concepts and the other shares only shallow patterns.

The study is most useful when model designers match pair similarity to task needs, because coordination-heavy tasks benefit from closer internal alignment while originality-heavy tasks may benefit from more difference.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small testbed with several model pairs and two game types: one that rewards strict coordination and one that rewards varied idea generation. Measure a layer-wise similarity score for each pair, then compare that score against task results for both game types.

The demo should show that high-similarity pairs win more often on coordination tasks while lower-similarity pairs produce broader outputs on originality tasks, because that is the paper's central tradeoff.
demo.closing: A convincing demo must show that pair selection should depend on the job, because the best partner for agreement is not always the best partner for broad exploration.
